title: LSEG Partners With Nvidia to Analyse Decades of Market Data in Seconds
excerpt: Using Nvidia GPU-accelerated computing, LSEG says years of Tick History — 110 trillion rows across 100 million instruments — can be analysed in seconds instead of hours, without copying the dataset.
body:
• London Stock Exchange Group (LSEG) announced on Wednesday a collaboration with Nvidia to help financial institutions analyse large volumes of historical market data far faster, using Nvidia GPU-accelerated computing.
  • Benchmarks cited by the companies show years of LSEG Tick History data can be analysed in seconds with Nvidia cuDF and Polars, down from hours, without creating another full copy of the dataset.
  • Tick History holds about 110 trillion rows across 100 million instruments, spanning more than 30 years and more than 580 exchanges, trading venues and contributors.
  • For readers in quant, trading and fintech roles: the change is aimed at intraday research as equity trading moves toward near 24-hour operation, not just overnight batch analysis after the close.

London Stock Exchange Group said on Wednesday it has partnered with Nvidia to help financial institutions process and analyse large volumes of historical market data faster and at scale, according to Reuters reporting carried by The Economic Times. The collaboration uses Nvidia cuDF for accelerated computing on Nvidia GPUs, LSEG said in its announcement covered by FX News Group.

LSEG, which operates the London Stock Exchange and provides data and analytics, has been expanding its offerings as AI changes how businesses trade and consume data, while retaining licences and control over that data. The new arrangement is designed to do the same: firms can run large-scale processing on Tick History datasets without creating another full copy of the underlying data, preserving the licences, permissions and controls that govern access.

"Customers want to work with detailed historical data at speed"

— Ron Lefferts, Co-Head of Data & Analytics, LSEG

What the technology changes

The collaboration forms part of what LSEG calls its Everywhere AI strategy, bringing its permissioned historical data closer to the computing environments already used for quantitative research, market analysis and AI. Benchmark analysis cited by the companies shows years of Tick History can be analysed in seconds using Nvidia cuDF and Polars, reducing processing time from hours to seconds.

The scale explains why speed matters. Tick History holds 110 trillion rows of data across 100 million instruments spanning more than 30 years and more than 580 exchanges, trading venues and contributors. Demand is also rising in real time: in the first half of 2026, traffic over LSEG's real-time network grew 29% versus the first half of 2025, reaching a new peak of 26 million messages per second in June, while customer API requests for Tick History data increased 48%.

Nvidia's Ioana Boier said, in the announcement, that AI is opening new ways to understand market behaviour across vast amounts of data, and that cuDF helps researchers analyse Tick History at scale without discarding the granular detail that makes it valuable.

Why firms want history, intraday

As equity trading moves towards near 24-hour operation, firms are moving away from legacy models that rely on loading data at the market close and running analytics overnight, LSEG said. Analysis on Nvidia's specialised processors, without creating copies of the dataset, could help study every trade and price quote in seconds, making research faster and closer to real time.

The intended uses are practical rather than experimental: quantitative research and strategy testing over longer histories and more venues, execution and market analysis including order-book reconstruction and assessments of pricing, liquidity and execution quality, and risk work such as scenario analysis and historical market replay. LSEG also presents it as a foundation for customers to apply their own analytical and AI models to governed data.

LSEG is the largest customer of Reuters, which provides news for its Workspace platform and other products, Reuters noted. The group also plans next year to launch LSE 24, a night-time trading venue for some exchange-traded products — a move that underlines the same shift toward longer trading hours driving the data announcement.

What to watch next

The announcement does not change Tick History's licensing model; if anything, it reinforces it. The pitch to banks, asset managers and trading firms is speed without surrendering control — deeper histories analysed closer to the point of decision, with permissions intact. For Indian-origin quants, data engineers and traders working in London, New York and Singapore, the practical test will be whether their firms adopt GPU-based pipelines and how much historical back-testing moves from overnight batches into the trading day itself.
